analysis_notes: The passage defines 啟發 as a 形號 that encompasses the high and low positions of musical sound “from beginning to end.” The definition presents the clef as an orienting sign that makes pitch position legible across the staff, rather than as a simple name for a graphic symbol. 啟發 has an established Chinese sense of opening or initiating: this wording foregrounds the operational mechanism of the clef on the five-line staff. Conceptually, this phrasing echoes the latin expression “principium scalae” found in Athanasius Kircher’s Musurgia Universalis (1650, Book 8, p. 49), thereby shedding light on the possible intertextual genealogy of the compilation. Alongside this semantic and intertextual genealogy, it is worth considering a potential phonetic dimension. Based on historical, the first character 啓 (qi) retained an unpalatalized velar initial [kʰ-] in early modern court Mandarin (as documented in Trigault’s 1626 Xiru Ermu Zi).   It is therefore possible that kʰifa was additionally intended as a partial phonetic approximation of the initial syllable of the Latin term clavis.

In the corrected draft, the concept of clavis signata is consistently rendered as qifa 啟發 (with the graphic variant 啟). In the fair copy, however, the first character appears as 啓 in the introduction, then shifts to the variant 啟 in the following chapter. This close juxtaposition may suggest the involvement of different hands.

In this passage, 品 occurs in 上中下三品, a three-part classification used “to clarify distinctions in 調.” The text explains the categories as three registers or levels—high, low, and level—and says they mark the tonal course of a piece. 品 therefore functions as a classifier of musical categories, not as a direct lexical equivalent of “clef.” Its broad Chinese semantic range includes class, rank, and kind; here the local definition narrows that range to an explicitly musical classification. The familiar classificatory force of 品 may have made the scheme legible to readers
排號 names a sign used at the head of the staff to identify the note or letter on which the clef is based. 號 marks the item as a sign; 排 may suggest ordering, arrangement, or placement.

analysis_notes: 排法 appears in the statement that two methods or arrangements are commonly used, one high and one low. In this context it seems to refer to the organization or use of clefs, not necessarily to an individual clef sign. The contrast between 排號 and 排法 is significant: Mateer can name both the visible sign and the method or arrangement through which signs organize notation.

"Hard" (gang 剛) is not originally a property of the clef itself, but identifies a musical category associated with the clef. The contrast with 柔啟發 and the related expressions 剛樂 and 柔樂 make a connection with the European durum/molle distinction plausible: this clef is called 'hard' because it is associated with the hard hexachord (hexachordum durum, with B♮). At the same time, a clef sign could be understood not merely as marking a pitch on the staff but as standing for the entire hexachord beginning on that pitch. Thus, gang qifa is the clef that implies the hard hexachord, rather than simply a label for high register (Picard & Thoraval 2014).

上品 is defined as an ascending, increasingly high 調 and illustrated with a sign. The text also relates that sign to 柔記 within the 剛柔 system and explains its use through the upward motion of the melody. The term combines a vertical adjective, 上, with 品, a classificatory noun. It is thus best read as “upper category” in the source’s own taxonomy. Its functional association with a treble-clef sign is supported by the notation and its placement, but “treble clef” is the modern analytical mapping rather than a literal translation of 上品.

高排 is introduced as the “high” member of a high/low distinction. 高 therefore identifies the relative register or position of the clef category, while 排 connects the expression to the arrangement of notation. The term is functionally aligned with the treble clef in this passage.

analysis_notes: 戊排 names the clef through the source’s explicit equivalence 戊（即G）: the transculturation process can be observed in the use of the 5th heavenly stem wu 戊 (halberd) to denote the 5th note (G) in the system introduced by Mateer. The previous passage in the chapter presents the association between the seven note letters(from C to B) and the first seven heavenly stems.

中啟發 is described as encompassing sounds without an extreme high or low, and as usable across multiple voice ranges. 中 therefore evokes a position between extremes and a capacity to mediate among ranges, in this case between 剛 and 柔. The text’s additional name 合性啟發 strengthens the idea of a clef that can accommodate or “fit” different vocal positions. The C-clef was indeed the principal movable clef of Renaissance and Baroque notation. It could be placed on different staff lines to represent soprano, mezzo-soprano, alto, tenor, and baritone ranges, allowing music to be notated with fewer ledger lines. If the sign and staff placement identify a C-clef, the modern label “alto clef” is useful for comparison, but the Chinese term itself is broader than the modern voice-specific name.

analysis_notes: 中品 is defined as a level in which the upward and downward tendencies are balanced or most even. The passage then specifies that its sign is usually recorded on the middle line, but may shift to the second or fourth line depending on the direction of the melody. 中 therefore names a relational center, not an invariant pitch or fixed staff position. The category’s flexibility is important: the sign’s position responds to musical movement, and the label organizes that use.

analysis_notes: The text explains 柔啟發 through its association with 悲怨類之柔音 and says that it is used in the lower range. The term therefore joins a qualitative musical category, 柔, to the same clef-naming expression 啟發 used elsewhere. The contrast with 剛啟發 suggests that the system organizes clefs through a 剛/柔 opposition as well as through register. The F-clef thus functions as the representative of the mollis hexachordal domain (Picard & Thoraval 2014). Its association with the grave register appears to be a pedagogical consequence of this assignment rather than the primary semantic content of the term.

下品 is defined through a descending movement from high to low and a sign placed on the fourth or fifth staff line. Its explanation emphasizes the sign’s capacity to encompass high, middle, and low sounds over a broad range. 下 therefore marks a direction or relative position within the system, while 品 places that distinction within a named taxonomy. This is not simply a social “lower rank”: the passage gives a specifically musical definition.

analysis_notes: 丁排 names the clef through the explicit equation 丁即F. The transculturation process can be observed in the use of the 4th heavenly stem ding to denote the 4th note (F) in the system introduced by Mateer. 丁's other dictionary senses (such as 'nail' fastener, 'male adult', 'robust', 'T-shaped',or 'to strike') do not explain the notation unless Mateer invokes them.

間歇形號 denotes a family of eight visible signs that indicate the extent of pauses in relation to musical rhythm and note duration. The passage explains how performers use the signs together with the music master’s gestures to stop and resume. 間歇 emphasizes interruption or intervals; 形號 foregrounds the visible notational form. Later on, the chapter further emphasizes the necessary presence of rests: 樂內不可不用間歇形號。奏大樂時有此間歇形號，則奏樂者詠歌間作，而聽之者乃覺和順而不厭矣！(GGZB 373, upper reproduction)

analysis_notes: Mateer’s appendix glossary identifies 正調 with “soprano,” which establishes the intended referent for this entry. The expression nevertheless carries a broader Chinese musical resonance: 正調 can designate a standard or principal tuning, mode, or musical framework in particular traditions. For instance, the expression could indicate a guqin’s tuning (also called 中呂均), while other Chinese music references use the term for a standard tuning contrasted with alternative tunings. In the work's contrast 正調之外另編副調, 正 is also relationally opposed to 副, supporting a sense of principal or primary category. The glossary’s reference should therefore be recorded as the source’s explicit analogous, while the possible resonance of 調 with tuning or mode remains an interpretive layer rather than a replacement gloss. This usage suggests that Mateer recruited a familiar musical expression to classify vocal parts, shifting its application from musical organization to voice type.

analysis_notes: Mateer lists 正品, 副品, 下品, and 上品, then identifies the singer of 正品 as a high-voiced woman. 正 contrasts with 副 and is best read here as principal or primary, not automatically as “orthodox” in the doctrinal sense. 品 functions as a category label and this wording evokes the taxonomy used in the Supplement for the clefs. However, in this case it is applied to vocal classification.  Mateer's glossary appended in the work explicitly related 品 to the English translation 'part'.

副品 is paired with 正品 and is associated in the text with a low-voiced woman. 副 marks a secondary, additional, or auxiliary relation; so, in this list, the label appears to distinguish a vocal category from the principal one. The term should be interpreted through the local taxonomy and the appendix’s possible gloss of 品, not through an assumed hierarchy among singers.
